status: Implemented; focused, default, Worker and explicit HTTP row-fallback validation passed
contract: Detach stable borrowed scanner data into independently owned backing before scanner advancement. Reserve container, property, traversal descriptor and binary-view storage before constructing it. Immutable scalar values receive retained charges. Preserve plain/null-prototype records, arrays, binary slices, timestamps and decimal scalars; reject cycles, accessors and unsupported custom prototypes.

integrationCases: Reused scanner row, nested object and binary storage detached before scanner mutation.
Winner ownership remains live while ordered batches are yielded; early consumer return releases it.
Candidate admission failure closes scanner and preserves sibling allocation.
Resumable scalar rows remain correct after scanner mutation.
Unsupported nested checkpoint serialization releases retained winners.
validation.remoteEvidence: Real wide-timestamp Parquet through a row-only parquetScanner adapter, four concurrent ordered/offset queries over HTTP 206 and ignored-range 200 responses, repeated after cache reuse. Shared pool peak bounded and final eviction returns usage to zero. Worker suite passed, but the new borrowed-row adapter is HTTP-only.

limits: Bounded and ordinary unlimited collectOrderedMatches now own detached rows through their consumers. Stateful sort runs, checkpoint deserialize/serialize allocations, hive merge scratch and result projection/output admission remain open.
Input data properties must remain stable during synchronous traversal; proxies and arbitrary object behavior have no detachment guarantee.
Charge units and traversal admission do not establish total VM heap bounds or expose hidden immutable-string backing size.
Supported scanner value shapes must be reconciled with public compatibility before query integration; unsupported prototypes are not silently flattened.
Rejected-candidate copy avoidance and benchmark evidence: docs/validation/row-top-k-precheck-2026-11-13.json.
testContractClarification: Existing exact serialized-size tests now specify a separate 65536-byte allocation allowance. Their serialized boundaries and expected errors are unchanged; production allocation/serialized limits were not relaxed.
